name: Physical modelling: Karplus-Strong plucks, bowed/struck strings, modal and comb resonators
goal: Synthesize plucked, bowed, struck and resonant instruments by exciting delay lines, comb filters and modal resonator banks with noise or clicks, controlling damping, brightness and body.

theory: A delay line of length 1/f with a low-pass in its feedback loop is a string: high harmonics decay faster. Excitation brightness = pick hardness; loop gain = sustain. Modal banks of inharmonic partials model bars, bells and plates.
prerequisites: Bit/sample-rate reducer, reverb, limiter, macro rack
Compressor, chorus and reverb for finishing
Delay with feedback and an in-loop low-pass (or build one)
Exciter source (noise burst generator, drum loop, synth pad, piano)
Filter with LFO (S&H + smoothing), ping-pong delay with feedback
Harmonic/spectral resonator (Web Audio: bank of high-Q bandpass filters or comb/modal resonators at harmonics of a note, implementation note)
MPE controller or pressure/Y-axis CC sources

Modal/physical-modelling synth with exciter + resonator sections (several free and paid options exist), or Web Audio: a bank of tuned BiquadFilter bandpass (high Q) or decaying sine partials excited by a short noise/impulse buffer (implementation note)
Modulation sources: velocity, envelopes, per-note random, key tracking
Noise source, bandpass/SVF filter, short envelope, velocity and key-pitch modulation, simple math (exp/invert)

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: Rendered part or recipe following the workflow

constraints: Portable recipe; not affiliated with any vendor; do not copy factory presets or sample packs.
Numbers in variants come from the source video transcripts; workflow steps are the consolidated mainstream practice.
Bring drums in early and avoid pitch wobble unless asked (user preferences from daily tests).

steps.action: Excite: short noise burst (pluck), continuous filtered noise (bow), click/mallet (strike).
Resonator: key-tracked delay/comb tuned to the note (Karplus-Strong), or modal bank with material-specific partial ratios.
Damping: low-pass in the loop and feedback 0.99-0.999 control decay; frequency-dependent decay for realism.
Brightness: pre-filter the excitation; velocity -> brightness and amplitude.
Body: add parallel combs/EQ for instrument body; MPE pressure -> bow noise level.
Scale-locked resonator banks or 12-voice strums for generative swarms; noise crackle into harmonic resonators for textures.
Hear the theory: run `/home/box/audio-tools/bin/python sample-lab/theory/karplus_strong.py` from the repo root and compare the sections; reuse its functions as a starting point for renders.
steps.expect: WAV in sample-lab/theory/out/ demonstrating the principle

verification: Render a short test and A/B against a reference at matched loudness
Run the generator and confirm it writes a WAV without error
Check mono compatibility and that no element masks the kick/bass

variants.name: Physically modelled bowed string: key-tracked noise exciters into a 100%-wet key-tracked comb, MPE pressure on gain/resonance, MPE timbre fading in a 3rd-harmonic comb, and a three-comb instrument body that retunes cello to bass, viola or violin
variants.goal: Build a playable bowed-string voice from synthesis only (no bow sample): a quiet noise exciter feeds a positive comb filter with full key tracking, maximum resonance, 100% wet and cutoff at C4 so it plays in the right octave. MPE pressure (through a shaped response curve) raises exciter gain and lifts comb resonance from about 80 for a scratchy light touch. MPE timbre crossfades in a second key-tracked comb at G5 (third harmonic, resonance ~40%) only near the top of the Y range. A fixed three-comb body (centre a little below 100 Hz, offsets of almost an octave and nearly three octaves, feedback ~15%, tone to taste, pans centred) sets the instrument size. Tame exciter bleed by keeping noise strongest near the played pitch: two S&H-noise oscillators, one optimised for the high end (low cut, key track +10) and one for the low end (high cut, key track −10). Delta beyond our existing noise→resonator and Karplus-style skills: MPE expression mapping plus key-tracked exciter colour and a body comb trio.
steps: Initialise the patch. Route a basic noise oscillator into filter 1 set to comb positive with key tracking full, resonance maximum, 100% wet and cutoff C4. Keep the noise level low and set the overall gain very low before first playing.

Add a concert-hall reverb, then set up an MSEG-style response curve driven by MPE pressure (loop off, rate disabled, phase ← pressure ~99%). Use it to raise exciter/output gain and to lift comb resonance from ~80 (unipolar) back toward full.

Add filter 2 as a second key-tracked comb at G5 (third harmonic of C4), resonance ~40%, filter mode with two filters in series/blend (S2-type), filter balance fully toward filter 1. Make a second curve named 'timbre' driven by MPE Y (≈49% because it reads as bipolar, base 50%) and shape it so the balance only moves toward filter 2 at the top of the Y range; add pressure to its resonance.

Add an instrument body with a three-comb FX block: pans 0, centre a little below 100 Hz (cello), offsets of almost an octave and closer to three octaves, feedback down to ~15%, tone low for a vintage recording sound or higher (or slightly less mix) for 'in the room'. Lower the mix of the upper combs so the centre resonates strongest.

Resize the instrument: move the body centre to ~50 Hz and lower noise colour for double bass; raise centre, noise colour and tone by ear for viola and further for violin. Play in the instrument's own range.

Tame noise: noise near the comb cutoff resonates nicely, noise far from it sounds like hiss. Key-track the noise colour upward. Better: mute the basic noise and use two S&H-noise oscillators (level ~−10, exciter gain ~−38 then ~−48), tune correlation/width by ear (width can give a formant-like bow character). Oscillator 1 handles high notes (low cut, key track +10) and oscillator 2 handles low notes (high cut, key track −10).
Optionally stack a cello-body convolution IR after the combs (watch the low-end build-up and EQ it), then fine-tune levels.

variants.name: Karplus-Strong pluck: noise-burst exciter into a key-tracked feedback delay with decay/damping and register compensation
variants.goal: Build a playable Karplus-Strong plucked string in any modular/Web Audio environment: a short pink-noise burst (bandpass-filtered, velocity-scaled, optionally stereo) excites a delay line tuned to one period of the note (delay = 1/f, e.g. ~7.64 ms at C3; halve per octave up via 2^(−n/12) scaling), with feedback as decay and a low-pass in the loop as damping, both velocity-scalable and key-tracked to even out low-vs-high note ring time.
steps: Build the exciter: pink noise (fuller than white) → bandpass SVF → a very short pluck envelope on level; add a velocity multiplier to scale excitation, and gain to keep long exciters in check.
Feed the burst into a delay with built-in feedback and an in-loop low-pass. Set delay = one period of the target fundamental (7.64 ms ≈ C3) and feedback high so it keeps resonating.

Key-track the delay: delay time must scale by 2^(−n/12) (n = semitones from the reference). Going up an octave halves delay; down an octave doubles it. Convert the note-pitch value to that factor (exp base 2, invert, offset so the reference note = no change) before feeding the delay-time modulation.
Exciter variations: use the envelope itself as the exciter (attack time changes tone like pluck position); widen the noise stereo for a lush tone; long exciter envelopes give a reverb-like bloom.

Map Decay → feedback (near unity = rings forever; low = unpitched thump) and Damping → loop low-pass (palm-mute-like). Optionally scale both by velocity (harder = longer ring/less damping); keep velocity amounts low—it is touchy.

Compensate register: at equal feedback low notes ring longer than high notes, so key-track feedback up for high notes and adjust damping in the opposite direction so decay and brightness feel even across the scale.
Experiment: feed other sounds as the exciter into the tuned delay for pitched resonant textures.

variants.name: Modal (partial-bank) physical-modelling voice: exciter into one or two resonators defined by a partial model, with material (decay vs frequency), tone (level tilt), hit (random partial emphasis), inharmonic stretch, parallel or series resonators, and velocity/random modulation for a playable mallet or string
variants.goal: Build a playable modal physical-modelling instrument from an exciter and a resonator made of tuned partials. Pick a partial model (string, beam, membrane, vibraphone, open tube or a manual partial list with 1 to 64 partials) and shape it with four relationships from the transcript: decay/release sets how long partials ring; material sets how fast high partials decay relative to low ones (muted vs glassy); tone sets partial level only (a static tilt, different from material); hit changes which partials are boosted at random, like plucking at a different position; and an inharmonic multiplier stretches or compresses partial spacing away from integer harmonics (metallic vs compressed). Choose the exciter (impulse, long exciter, noise): it mostly sets the attack, and a bass-heavy exciter mostly excites low partials. Run two resonators in parallel (blend) or in series (resonator 1 as an extended exciter, e.g. a short-decay drum head into a tube, with optional cross-feedback). Make it playable: velocity to level, material and exciter level; an envelope for a sharper attack over the ringing tail; subtle random on tone, stronger random on hit per note; key → layer gain to lift quiet high notes. More specific than our Karplus-Strong and comb-resonator skills: a modal partial bank with decay-vs-frequency and inharmonicity controls.
steps: Mute the resonators and raise the exciter's direct output to audition exciters (impulse, long exciter, noise). Then turn the direct output back down and enable resonator 1.
Pick a partial model and partial count for resonator 1 (start with the string model). Try beam, membrane, vibraphone and open tube to hear how partial patterns change the instrument.

Shape the partials: decay/release for ring time; material down = high partials die faster (muted), up = the opposite; tone = cut highs or lows by level only; hit = random partial emphasis (pluck position); inharmonic multiplier up = stretched, metallic partials, down = compressed partials.
Optional manual mode: edit partial positions and amplitudes (e.g. 4 partials), make two snapshots and use a ratio control to morph between them.

Add resonator 2. Parallel: same exciter into both, set level and balance. Series: exciter → R1 → R2; use R1 with a very short decay (drum head) as an extended exciter for a tube in R2. Raise cross-feedback strength carefully.
Optionally layer the two basic oscillators and route chosen sources through two filters (series or parallel), e.g. filter only the oscillators. Use the second layer for a second, different sound.

Make it playable: velocity → resonator level, material (louder = more high partials) and exciter level; envelope 1 with a fast attack and low sustain/decay → level for a prominent attack over the tail; subtle random → tone; per-note random → hit; for a vibraphone, slow sine LFO → pitch at a very small depth.
Finish: low-cut a resonator if it gets muddy, then stereo widener, compressor, chorus and reverb. If high notes are quieter, map key tracking → layer gain.

variants.name: Effects-only melodic instrument: crackle/noise source → smoothed-random filter → ping-pong feedback delay → spectral harmonic resonator (note, decay, harmonic count, pitch mod) → 'smudge' lo-fi/unison macro → reverb → limiter
variants.goal: Make a playable wind-chime / abstract atmosphere instrument from effects only. Generate vinyl-style crackle (only its density is mapped), or feed any external audio (drums, vocals). Filter it with a resampling-type filter whose cutoff is moved by a sample-and-hold LFO smoothed 100% (random glides), with ~10% drive. Multiply it with a ping-pong delay (6/16, 5/16, down to triplets) at high feedback. Excite a harmonic spectral resonator in note mode, using the granular engine with input quantised, unison 2 and low-damp fixed at 15%. Map fundamental note, decay (blips vs pads), number of harmonics (minimum 6; more = brighter and higher, with high-damp tied to the same macro) and pitch-mod amount (up to 1 semitone) and rate. A 'smudge' macro raises resonator unison spread together with bit/sample-rate reduction (0 = 18 kHz/16-bit, i.e. off). Finish with reverb (size 100, diffusion-network filter on) on time + amount macros, a limiter, macro snapshots and randomisation that excludes note, input level and reverb. Delta vs our click-train comb texture: noise conditioning chain + harmonic resonator macro design.
steps: Create an effects rack (audio-effect track) with 16 macros. First device: crackle/noise generator; map only its density (crackle level) to a macro. Alternatively route external audio (e.g. bongo drums, vocals) into the rack.

Add a filter in a resampling/character mode, LFO wave sample-and-hold with smoothing 100%, drive ~10%. Map cutoff, LFO amount and LFO rate to macros to sculpt which parts of the noise spectrum excite the resonator.
Add a ping-pong delay at 100% wet. Map delay time (e.g. 6/16, 5/16, limited down to triplets for ambient use), a small L/R delay offset for stereo interest, and feedback (high).

Add the spectral resonator: note mode, granular engine, quantise input on, unison 2, low damp fixed ~15% (cuts boomy lows). Map fundamental note, decay, number of harmonics (min 6) plus high damp on the same macro, pitch-mod amount (up to 1 st) and rate, and input level.
Add a bit/sample-rate reducer after the resonator. Make one 'smudge' macro that raises the resonator's unison spread, lowers bit depth and lowers sample rate together (0 = 18 kHz/16-bit, i.e. off).
Add reverb (size 100, diffusion-network filter on) and map decay time and dry/wet, then a final limiter to catch peaks.
Play it: short decay for plucks and blips, long decay for pads. Save macro snapshots of good settings and randomise for new territory, with note, input level and reverb excluded from randomisation.

variants.name: Scale-locked resonator bank as an instrument: up to 12 tuned resonator voices on a root and scale (e.g. D minor 9, 6 voices, octave 3), excited by a stereo noise burst or drums, with motion modes (wave, strum, arpeggio, swarm), feedback/decay/damping/spread/diffusion and gated live-key voicing
variants.goal: Use a bank of tuned resonators as a playable texture generator. Tune all voices to a root note and scale chord (example: root D, minor 9, 6 voices in octave 3) and pick a resonator model (string, bar, glass harmonica, bowl, membrane, bell, plate, tube; strings add position and brightness). Excite it with a short stereo white-noise burst (ADSR with no sustain, two steps), kicks, snares, hats, pads or piano. Animate which voices sound with a motion mode: wave (amplitude, per-voice frequency spread, phase, rate), strum (spread, curvature, direction up/down/alternate, alternate rate), arpeggio (rate, gate, up/down/up-down/random) or swarm (centre, cohesion, rate). Shape the tail with feedback, decay, damping, stereo spread and diffusion, plus vibrato, and switch to live keys or gated mode to set voices from held chords. More specific than our single harmonic-resonator and noise-crackle skills: a multi-voice scale bank with voice-motion sequencing.
steps: Insert the resonator bank on a source. Set root (lockable) and scale, then the number of voices and octave (example D minor 9, 6 voices, octave 3).
Choose a resonator model; test kick, snare and hats through it, trimming output when loud. On string models also set position and brightness.
Build a noise exciter: an ADSR-gated stereo white-noise generator with no sustain, triggered on two steps of a sequencer.

Pick a motion mode. Wave: adjust amplitude, per-voice frequency spread (more chaotic), phase and rate. Strum: spread, curvature, direction (one way, opposite, alternating) and alternate rate. Arp: rate, gate, up/down/up-down/random. Swarm: centre, cohesion (tight to loose) and rate. Set steps and window size, tempo-synced if wanted, and randomise.
Shape the tail: feedback, decay, damping, stereo spread, diffusion; add vibrato rate/depth; balance dry/wet.
Switch to live keys so the held notes set the voices (one note, two notes, four notes), or gated mode to sound only while keys are held. Try a pad or piano as input with mix fully wet.

variants.name: Struck-string physical-model synth controls that differ from subtractive synthesis: brightness set before the strike (not a filter), frequency-dependent decay (cutoff + slope) instead of sustain, strike point, harmonicity, three-string unison, and mallet-bounce retriggers at different note values per layer for sequenced polyrhythmic patches
variants.goal: Design pads, basses and keys on a struck/plucked physical model and know which controls behave unlike a subtractive synth. Plucking brightness changes a sine-like tone into a saw-like one but only at the strike: lowering it while a note rings does nothing, so put a real filter after the model for sweeps. There is no sustain: decay and release plus a decay cutoff and slope define how partials above the cutoff die faster (low cutoff + high slope = more decay). Strike point acts like the pick position; harmonicity moves the tone from harmonic to inharmonic (steel-drum-like with more bloom); unison width detunes the three strings per note; smear softens transients. Mallet bounce makes a held note re-strike itself; stacking layers with different bounce values (dotted half, quarter, eight beats in the demo) gives sequenced, polyrhythmic patterns without a sequencer. Delta beyond our modal-partial skill: decay slope, pre-strike brightness and mallet-bounce layering.
steps: Start from a sine-like init voice. Raise plucking/strike brightness to move toward a bright, saw-like tone. Test that turning it down while a note rings does not change that note.
Edit the harmonic profile (raise some partials, lower others) for a new basic colour, and set unison width to detune the three strings per note for synth-style thickness.

Shape length: fast attack for keys or slower for pads; decay and release for ring time. Set the decay cutoff and slope: partials above the cutoff die faster as slope rises (low cutoff + high slope = shortest, darkest tail).
Set strike point (like pick position) and harmonicity (harmonic → inharmonic). With higher brightness and more bloom, inharmonic settings give steel-drum-like tones. Use smear to soften transients.
Enable mallet bounce so a held note re-strikes; adjust bounce rate and decay over time.

Build a sequenced patch with 2–3 layers and different bounce note values (e.g. dotted half, quarter, 8 beats). Turning off bounce on one layer will not stop the pattern while the other layers still bounce.
Map mod wheel → LFO rate, vibrato and tremolo depth. Finish with EQ and effects (chorus, phaser, delay, compression) and a post filter if you need cutoff sweeps.
